findings.title: Persist each transaction directory name before starting lifecycle side effects
findings.trigger: On a Linux filesystem, power loss after a new lifecycle journal is written and services/pointers/definitions have changed, but before the transaction directory entry happens to reach durable storage.
findings.evidence: common.mkdir only creates/chmods/chowns a directory (common.py:75-80). write_json uses atomic_write, whose sole directory barrier is the immediate file parent (common.py:53-72). The release, provider, HTTPS, configuration-layer and uninstall paths create state/transactions/<id> and flush state.json inside it, but never fsync state/transactions before side effects or their terminal record. Consequently the retained journal can disappear while durable pointer/config/unit changes survive. The strongest complete chain is uninstall_services: mkdir journal.parent (209), write journal (212), publish config/uninstalled.json referring to its ID (213-214), stop/remove units and sudo entry (220-228), terminal journal and durable uninstalled marker (234-236). restore_services then requires that missing journal and its before image. Ordinary pending transaction discovery can also miss a lost release/provider/config/HTTPS transaction.

affectedLocations.behavior: release prepared journal precedes stop; no transactions-parent barrier through committed write at408
provider prepared journal precedes stop/select; no transactions-parent barrier through committed write at458
configuration-layer journal precedes barriers and stop; no transactions-parent barrier through committed write at302
uninstall marker refers to an unflushed transaction-directory name before definitions are durably removed
same collection publication defect for input/cache/prepared build evidence through prepared.json at345; release tree and manifest themselves have separate correct barriers

findings.impact: Recovery material and transaction discovery are not crash-durable. A successful uninstall can retain an uninstalled marker while losing the only saved definitions required by restore-services; interrupted mutations can become undiscoverable.
findings.recommendation: Use a shared durable directory publication operation that verifies trusted ancestry and flushes the directory plus its parent chain, including existing directories on interrupted retry. Require it before the first dependent side effect. Add fault-injection assertions that a failed parent barrier prevents stop, pointer/config selection and uninstall deletion.
findings.verification: Fresh full source reads and caller/terminal-write tracing. No power-cut simulation or live service execution was performed.

findings.title: Make the root management receipt directory durable before dispatching a mutation
findings.trigger: The first root management mutation creates state/receipts, reaches the requested side effect, and the machine loses power before the new receipts directory entry is durably published in state.
findings.evidence: dispatch creates receipts at625 and atomically writes running at626, then dispatches restart/provider changes and writes completed at666. Both write_json calls only fsync receipts, not state. Installation build_plan does not precreate receipts (install_recovery.py:304-313). There is no later fsync(state) in this dispatch chain. preflight_mutation regards an absent receipt as new at manager.py:583-609; operation/read reports not_received for an absent file at655.
findings.impact: A management action may finish but its durable idempotency record can disappear. Later root reconciliation returns not_received and a repeated original request can execute again, violating the manager receipt contract.
findings.recommendation: Durably publish the receipts directory and relevant ancestors before the initial running receipt and before entering any action. Preserve replay behavior when the directory already exists after an interrupted attempt; test parent fsync failure prevents invocation.
findings.verification: Fresh semantic read of initialization, mutation preflight, dispatch, receipt lookup and atomic write implementation. This concerns the root manager receipt layer, not a claim that gateway SQLite receipts lack their own persistence.

findings.title: Flush publication-directory ancestry before acknowledging retained generations and initial installation
findings.trigger: Power loss after selecting a newly staged certificate/CA, saving the first provider profile, or completing an installation whose managed top-level containers were newly created.
findings.evidence: stage_tls creates config/tls/<revision> and atomic-writes the files (333-341); stage_tls_ca does the same under tls-ca (376-383). Those writes flush only the revision directory. setup_https later durably writes Caddyfile, instance.json and https.json and commits (565-605), but never flushes tls or tls-ca, so the selected revision name can be lost. Profiles.save creates config/provider-profiles then writes the profile (provider_lifecycle.py:79-83); the save-only provider action returns immediately (manager.py:419-426) and never flushes config, so the first saved collection can disappear. initialize_recorded precreates app.parent/state.parent/control.parent (install_recovery.py:391-393) without flushing their parents, while root_lock creates config.parent (37) without flushing its parent before the initialization record is relied upon. CreationPlan publishes children and flushes their immediate parents (294), which does not persist the precreated container names in /opt, /var/lib or /usr/lib. Existing-plan entries return after verify (250-253), so retry also cannot be used as a guaranteed missing publication barrier.

affectedLocations.behavior: initial configuration-container ancestry and initial recovery record
new installation containers acknowledged after only descendant publication
existing verified entries skip a publication barrier during retry

findings.impact: A successfully selected TLS revision can be absent at reboot and prevent Caddy/HTTPS health startup; an acknowledged saved profile or a newly created installation container can disappear despite its files having been flushed.
findings.recommendation: Centralize trusted durable directory creation/publication, flush every newly created ancestor and re-establish missing barriers on retry before references or successful results are exposed. Keep initial lock creation ownership/symlink validation intact. Exercise TLS/CA and first-profile ordering plus initial container/retry paths with injected fsync failures.
findings.verification: Fresh full semantic reads, traced all generation publishers. ProviderStore.select explicitly flushes providers at provider.py:286, control update explicitly flushes record/barrier parents and transaction collection, request staging flushes its collection, workspace helpers use descriptor-relative parent barriers, and publish_release flushes releases and app. Those paths were not mislabeled as equivalent committed-generation failures. No physical crash test was performed.

methodDetails.independence: Fresh read-only audit of the frozen round2 inventory. No previous audit report was adopted as a conclusion; no old sibling source, Git history, personal credentials, retired host110 or running main services were accessed. AGENTS.md was read; the user-authorized two-clean-round gate overrides its default three.
methodDetails.semanticRead: All 154 assigned files other than the two explicitly listed generated/lock structural files were fully read in bounded sections. Read-span coverage and per-file SHA-256 were rechecked. This includes all 93 Python source/test files, all deployment modules and shell entrypoint, deployment/root fixtures and standalone probes, every assigned tooling/CI script and test, package/workspace/configuration files, deployment/recovery/product/architecture documentation and small evidence records. The source and test review traced validation, ownership, side-effect order, publication/compensation boundaries, idempotency/recovery, resource bounds, provider/config/HTTPS interfaces, installation/upgrades/uninstall and release/CI gating. Historical evidence was assessed for truthful scope/limitations, not treated as fresh test execution.
methodDetails.lockfile: pnpm-lock.yaml was read completely by a restricted structural reader that consumed every nonblank line, rejected unsupported constructs/duplicate block keys, checked all package SHA512 integrities, all 336 package/snapshot identities and all 623 dependency edges. All 21 direct pins were matched to package.json; overrides and importer/settings were manually inspected. This is generated dependency graph validation, not a semantic security audit of downloaded third-party package contents or an online vulnerability scan.

All 50 unique evidence-group assessments and 15 additional-workflow assessments plus metadata/limits were manually read. Historical hash references were syntax/path checked, not asserted to match the current moving-source provenance snapshot; this generated mapping was not counted as independent acceptance of every runtime/web implementation.
methodDetails.staticValidation: Parsed all 93 assigned Python files with ast.parse using the bundled Python runtime; zero parse errors. No tests (full or targeted), builds, dependency installs, service changes, external inference or external integrations were executed in this audit.
methodDetails.snapshot: Ran node scripts/snapshot.mjs at the end and recomputed the same snapshot again immediately before report construction: 1,877 files, digest unchanged. Every assigned file was SHA-256 hashed and matched its read or structural-validation digest.
limitations: No physical power-loss filesystem experiment was run; durability findings follow the explicit POSIX fsync ordering in source.
No Linux/systemd, live public DNS/ACME/certificate/browser acceptance, external provider/account/MCP integration or third-party package execution was attempted.
This report is complete for its assigned 156-file scope and has actionable findings; it is not a clean audit round.
